title: Garlic Butter Pasta
blurb: Five ingredients, one pan, and better than it has any right to be.
method: Boil the pasta in well-salted water. Save a cup of the water before draining.
Melt the butter in a pan over low heat. Add the garlic and cook gently until soft, not brown.
Add the drained pasta and a splash of the pasta water. Toss until glossy.
Stir through the parsley. Serve with parmesan and lots of pepper.

title: Overnight Oats
ingredients: Fruit, nuts, or seeds to top
method: Stir the oats, milk, yoghurt and honey together in a jar.
Cover and leave in the fridge overnight.
In the morning, loosen with a little more milk and add your toppings.

title: Meatloaf
ingredients: 1 lb ground beef (the family version uses 3 lbs — see notes)
method: Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C).
Beat the eggs before anything else goes in.
Chop the onion and celery. They go in raw.
Mix everything together — the ketchup and mustard go into the mix.
Shape into a loaf, either in a loaf pan or free-form on a tray.
Bake for 1 hour.
notes: The family version: 3 lbs of beef, and ketchup spread on top before it goes in the oven. This version is 1 lb and no ketchup on top.
Loaf pan or free-form both work. Free-form gives you more crust; a pan means it sits in its own fat.
No quantities were recorded for the onion, celery, garlic or breadcrumbs — go by feel.

CHECK: the 1-hour bake probably belongs to one of the two sizes rather than both. A 1 lb loaf is usually done well before an hour, and 3 lbs takes longer. Worth checking the middle hits 160°F the next time either gets made, and writing the real time in here.
OPEN: does the 2 eggs go with the 1 lb version or the 3 lb one?

title: Roasted Potatoes
ingredients: Potatoes — peeled, or red potatoes with the skins left on
method: Cut the potatoes into pieces.
Toss with olive oil, garlic powder, salt and pepper.
Roast at 350°F (175°C) for 20 minutes.
notes: Temperature confirmed at 350°F by the family member who makes these. It wasn't written on the original recipe.

CHECK: at 350°F, potato chunks usually want 45–60 minutes rather than 20. Something reconciles the two — most likely the pieces are cut smaller or thinner than a standard chunk. Worth asking how big they cut them.
Until that's settled, treat the 20 minutes as a first check rather than a finish time — go by a fork going in easily and the edges browning.

title: American Spaghetti and Meatballs
ingredients: Spaghetti — not on the original list, quantity to confirm
1 egg — the only binder, no breadcrumbs
Tomato soup — made up as normal soup (if condensed, add water per the can)
method: Make up the tomato soup as normal soup — if it's condensed, add the water the can calls for. Melt the American cheese or Velveeta into it.
Mix the ground beef with the egg, salt, pepper and celery salt or celery seed. No breadcrumbs.
Roll into meatballs.
Drop the raw meatballs into the soup and cheese mixture and cook them in it.
Boil the spaghetti.
Serve the meatballs and sauce over the spaghetti.
notes: This is the tomato-soup-and-melted-cheese style, not an Italian red sauce. That's the dish, not a substitution.
No breadcrumbs — deliberate, not an omission. The egg is the only binder.
The meatballs go in raw and cook in the sauce, so the sauce takes on flavour from the beef. They're never browned.
General technique, not from the recipe: raw meatballs are fragile until they've set, so leave them alone for the first few minutes rather than stirring.
No quantities were recorded beyond the one egg.

title: Sour Cucumbers
time: Half an hour soaking, then a few minutes
method: Slice the cucumbers.
Soak the slices in salt water for half an hour.
Tip into a colander and squeeze really tight to get the water out.
Slice the onions.
Mix the cucumbers and onions with sour cream, salt and pepper.
notes: No vinegar — checked, not an omission. The sour comes from the sour cream.
The soak and the hard squeeze are the whole trick — they pull the water out of the cucumbers so the sour cream stays thick instead of turning into a puddle. Don't shortcut either.
Squeeze harder than feels reasonable. The cucumbers will look wrung out and that's correct.
How the onions are cut wasn't recorded. Thin is the safer default — raw onion goes strong in sour cream if the pieces are big. Write down what you end up liking.
